fixes.explanation: A hundred, baker! Genesis 21:5 says Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him. Verse 2 says it happened at the very time God had promised. That's the detail to hold onto.

Close, but that's a different day in Abraham's life, friend. He was seventy-five when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4). When Isaac is born, Genesis 21:5 says he's a hundred. Seventy-five is the number to leave behind here.

That's it, baker. Sarah says, "God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me." She says everyone who hears, so this is laughter meant to be shared. I think that's joy too big to keep to herself.

Let's look again, friend. Sarah asks, "Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?" It's a question, and she never says anyone could have told him. Then she adds, "Yet I have borne him a son in his old age." I think she's still amazed that it happened.

Right, baker. Sarah asks, "Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?" She never says anyone could have. Her next words are, "Yet I have borne him a son in his old age." I think she's still shaking her head at it.
A great feast, baker! Genesis 21:8 says Abraham held it on the day Isaac was weaned. The child grew, and then came the day for the table. A feast with a few cookies on it sounds like my kind of day.

Mocking, baker. Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son. Hagar is Sarah's maidservant (Genesis 16:1), and her son is Ishmael. The text names the mocking, so that's the word we go with.

The text doesn't mention any shoving, friend. Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son. Hagar is Sarah's maidservant (Genesis 16:1), and her son is Ishmael. So the word is mocking.

It's more than that, friend. Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son. Hagar is Sarah's maidservant (Genesis 16:1), and her son is Ishmael. Mocking is doing something, and ignoring is doing nothing.

Beersheba, baker! Genesis 21:14 says Hagar left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba. Wandered is the word the text uses. She went with bread and a skin of water on her shoulders, and the boy went with her.

Yes, baker. She says, "I cannot bear to watch the boy die!" (Genesis 21:16). Then she sits about a bowshot away and weeps. I think that's a mother in deep anguish. It's a heavy moment, and I'd let it be heavy.

True, baker. The angel says, "Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies." (Genesis 21:17). God heard the boy's voice out there in the wilderness. That's the comfort in the line.

That's it, baker. The angel says, "Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand…" (Genesis 21:18). Hagar is told to lift him up and take his hand. After all the weeping, it's a gentle push forward.
Egypt, baker! Genesis 21:21 says Ishmael's mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt. Back in verse 9, the text calls his mother "Hagar the Egyptian." So Egypt shows up in both places.
